reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases / WHO guidance on onchocerciasis
clinicalPearls: Caused by the filarial nematode Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by the bite of Simulium blackflies that breed in fast-flowing rivers, hence 'river blindness'
Chronic infection produces intensely itchy dermatitis, altered skin pigmentation ('leopard skin'), skin atrophy, and firm subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas) housing adult worms
Microfilariae migrating to the eye cause keratitis, iritis, chorioretinitis, and optic atrophy, leading to progressive and potentially irreversible blindness
The endosymbiotic bacterium Wolbachia within the worm drives much of the inflammatory response, making doxycycline for Wolbachia a useful adjunct that also sterilises adult female worms
Diagnosis is classically by skin snips examined for emerging microfilariae, supported by nodule examination and antigen/antibody or PCR testing
Ivermectin is the mainstay microfilaricidal treatment and the basis of mass drug administration control programmes, given repeatedly as it does not reliably kill adult worms
Ivermectin can precipitate a severe reaction in patients heavily co-infected with Loa loa, so loiasis must be considered in co-endemic areas before treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Onchocerciasis results from infection with Onchocerca volvulus. Infective larvae are introduced by biting Simulium blackflies and mature into adult worms that reside coiled within fibrous subcutaneous nodules. Adult females release large numbers of microfilariae that migrate through the skin, connective tissue, and eye. Most disease is driven not by the live microfilariae but by the inflammatory reaction to dying microfilariae and to their endosymbiotic Wolbachia bacteria, which provoke dermal and ocular inflammation. In the eye, repeated microfilarial death causes punctate then sclerosing keratitis, anterior uveitis, and posterior segment damage, culminating in blindness. In the skin, chronic inflammation produces pruritus, depigmentation, and atrophy. Killing microfilariae abruptly, as with treatment, can intensify this inflammatory response (the Mazzotti reaction).
additionalDifferentials: Scabies and other causes of chronic pruritic dermatitis
Other causes of chorioretinitis or anterior uveitis
additionalInvestigations: Skin snips examined microscopically for emerging microfilariae
Palpation and examination or excision of subcutaneous nodules for adult worms
Slit-lamp examination for microfilariae and ocular inflammatory changes
PCR assays on skin snips for species confirmation
Assessment for Loa loa co-infection in co-endemic areas before treatment
redFlags: Ocular involvement threatening progressive or irreversible visual loss
Severe Mazzotti reaction after microfilaricidal treatment
Risk of severe reaction if ivermectin is given with high Loa loa co-infection
Extensive sight-threatening keratitis or optic atrophy
reference.prognosis: With repeated ivermectin therapy and vector control, transmission and morbidity can be greatly reduced; however, established ocular damage and optic atrophy are irreversible, and untreated chronic infection remains a leading infective cause of blindness.
pitfalls: Giving ivermectin without excluding heavy Loa loa co-infection in co-endemic regions
Expecting a single course of ivermectin to cure infection despite persistence of adult worms
Underestimating the sight-threatening potential of ocular microfilariae
Failing to anticipate and manage the Mazzotti reaction after treatment
management: Microfilaricidal treatment with ivermectin is the mainstay, given repeatedly at intervals because it does not reliably kill the adult worms
Add doxycycline to target the endosymbiotic Wolbachia, which sterilises and eventually kills adult female worms and dampens the inflammatory reaction
Exclude Loa loa co-infection in co-endemic areas before ivermectin, given the risk of severe encephalopathic reactions with high loiasis microfilaraemia
Provide symptomatic dermatological care for pruritus and dermatitis with antihistamines and emollients
Undertake regular slit-lamp ophthalmic surveillance for keratitis and uveitis, treating ocular inflammation to limit progression to irreversible blindness
Excise symptomatic subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas), particularly those on the head
Support mass drug administration and Simulium vector control as the basis of community-level transmission reduction
